title: The Journey of Water
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Water covers about seventy per cent of the surface of the Earth, but almost all of it is in the oceans and is too salty to drink. Only about three per cent is fresh, and most of that is locked in ice at the poles and in glaciers, or lies deep underground. The small amount that remains in rivers, lakes and the air is, however, enough to support all life on land, because water is not used up. It moves continuously between the oceans, the air and the land in a process called the water cycle, which has been working for billions of years and which has no real beginning or end.

The cycle is driven by the sun. Its heat warms the surface of oceans, lakes and rivers, and some of the liquid water turns into an invisible gas called water vapour. This change is called evaporation. About eighty-six per cent of all evaporation takes place over the oceans, and it happens faster when the weather is hot, dry and windy. Plants also release vapour through tiny holes in their leaves, a process known as transpiration. A single large tree can release hundreds of litres of water into the air on a hot day, so forests have an important effect on the climate and on the amount of rain that falls nearby.

As the water vapour rises, it meets colder air and cools. Cool air cannot hold as much vapour as warm air, so the vapour turns back into tiny drops of liquid water, a change called condensation. The drops gather around specks of dust, salt or smoke in the air and form clouds. Fog is simply a cloud that touches the ground. The drops in a cloud are so small and light that they stay in the air, and a typical cloud may contain hundreds of tonnes of water. Clouds are carried over great distances by the wind, which is how water that evaporated from the sea can fall on a mountain hundreds of kilometres from the coast.

When the drops in a cloud join together and become too heavy to float, they fall as precipitation. This may be rain, snow, sleet or hail, depending on the temperature of the air through which the water falls. Snow forms when the air is below freezing, and hail forms when strong currents carry drops up and down inside a storm cloud so that layers of ice build up around them. The amount of precipitation varies enormously around the world. Some places in the desert may receive less than twenty millimetres in a year, while a few mountain villages in tropical regions receive more than ten metres, which is the reason why some regions flood and others suffer from drought.

Rain that reaches the ground follows several routes. Some runs over the surface into streams and rivers, which carry it back to the sea; this is known as runoff. Some soaks into the soil, where it feeds plants or sinks deeper to become groundwater, stored in layers of rock called aquifers. Snow and ice can hold water for thousands of years before they melt. The time that a water molecule spends in each place differs greatly: a drop may stay in the atmosphere for about nine days, but in a deep aquifer or a large ice sheet it may remain for ten thousand years or more.

People have changed the cycle in many ways. Dams store water and slow rivers, irrigation sends large amounts of water into the air from fields, and cities cover the ground with concrete, so that rain runs off quickly instead of soaking in. Dr Helena Okafor, a hydrologist, says that the greatest change is the removal of groundwater: in many regions people now pump water from aquifers far faster than rain can refill them. She warns that wells in these areas may run dry within a generation, and that careful management of water is more urgent than ever for farmers, cities and industry alike.

Climate change is also altering the cycle. A warmer atmosphere holds more water vapour, which means that storms can produce heavier rain, and floods are becoming more common in many regions. At the same time, higher temperatures cause faster evaporation from soil, making droughts longer and more severe. Mountain glaciers, which act as natural reservoirs by storing winter snow and releasing it slowly in summer, are shrinking in most parts of the world. Scientists are working to measure these changes with satellites, which can track clouds, rainfall and even the level of groundwater from space, and to use the data to plan for the future.
